title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method
authors: Yuhe Wang, Zhu Wang, Min Wang
abstract: Physics-informed machine learning has become a major direction in predictive modeling of fluid dynamics, combining governing physics with learned representations. Yet prevailing formulations neither guarantee that small PDE-residual losses imply small solution errors nor scale effectively with increasing problem size. Here we present the neural basis method (NBM) as a new approach for Navier--Stokes dynamics. NBM is built on a ``representation-then-projection'' principle: fixed neural bases define the representation space, while projection of the governing equations determines the expansion coefficients. The same bases define common coordinates for the parametric solution manifold, recasting operator learning as a parameter-to-coefficient mapping and enabling scalability by removing explicit spatial dependence. For incompressible flow, NBM yields a velocity-only formulation whose residual provides an a posteriori velocity-error estimate, establishing a certified, data-free training objective for coefficient learning. Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability of NBM, with substantial improvements over baselines.

infographic.key_insight: The neural basis method separates fixed neural representations from physics-based coefficient determination to solve and learn Navier–Stokes dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared basis coordinates enable parameter-to-coefficient learning without explicit spatial inputs, offering a scalable approach to parametric flow prediction.
method: Define the solution space using fixed neural basis functions.
Project governing equations onto this space to determine expansion coefficients.
Learn parameter-to-coefficient maps using a velocity-only residual with an a posteriori velocity-error estimate.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical analysis and numerical experiments showing improvements over baselines in accuracy, efficiency, generalization, and scalability, but gives no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on how well the fixed neural bases represent flows beyond the evaluated parameter regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Solving and Learning Navier-Stokes Dynamics with the Neural Basis Method

title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI
authors: Jiawei Chen, Xiang I. A. Yang, Ping He
abstract: Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. Four large language model (LLM) agents then propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations and generate scripts for CFD simulations. The Discovery Agent infers the vortex axis from various vortex-identification methods. The candidates are tested on four cases spanning canonical and engineering flows: a flat plate, a backward-facing step, a free shear layer, and an iced airfoil. For all test cases, the best candidate consistently outperforms the standard length scale based on the maximum cell size. Its accuracy is similar to, or slightly better than, that of the expert-designed shear-layer-adapted length scale. Each agentic discovery run takes about 25 minutes on average, excluding the CFD simulations. These results show that LLM-based reasoning can significantly accelerate the discovery of physically interpretable turbulence models and reduce reliance on manual expert formulation.

infographic.key_insight: DEScover uses four LLM agents to discover physically interpretable DES subgrid length scales based on grid width normal to the local vortex axis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could accelerate turbulence-model development while improving DES accuracy over the standard maximum-cell-size length scale.
method: Start with a user-specified physical modeling idea.
Use four agents to propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations.
Infer vortex axes using vortex-identification methods and generate CFD simulation scripts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across a flat plate, backward-facing step, free shear layer, and iced airfoil, the best candidate consistently outperformed the standard length scale and matched or slightly exceeded an expert-designed shear-layer-adapted alternative.
infographic.watch_item: The reported average discovery time of about 25 minutes excludes CFD simulations, and performance beyond the four tested cases remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI

title: When does boundary-condition uncertainty outweigh thermal and vegetation effects in street canyon flow? A global sensitivity analysis of input uncertainty
authors: Albert Moreno Català, Joan Calafell Sandiumenge, Nikolaj T. Mücke, Jan Mateu Armengol
abstract: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is increasingly used to resolve wind, heat, and pollution patterns in cities with high fidelity but high computational cost. Thermal effects and vegetation are often neglected despite being important drivers, yet their influence may be masked by variability from other uncertain inputs. This work determines how precisely model parameters and boundary conditions must be known for these effects to govern output uncertainty in the velocity, temperature, and concentration fields of a two-dimensional street canyon. A global Sobol analysis of 24 parameters is made tractable by a surrogate trained on Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations, combining principal component analysis (PCA) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Two ventilation regimes assess the variance due to thermal and vegetation parameters as uncertainty in all other inputs is progressively reduced. At typical uncertainty levels, turbulence closure constants and inflow turbulence profiles govern variability in all three fields in both regimes. Under weak ventilation, solar forcing becomes the main source of temperature variability once the remaining uncertainties are halved, and of concentration variance once they are reduced to a quarter (about $\pm11\%$ for the dominant closure constant and $\pm12\%$ for the emission rate). In contrast, vegetation contributes significantly at typical uncertainty levels. Under strong ventilation, however, the canopy never overtakes the closure constants, even when the dominant one is known to $\pm5\%$. Spatially, both effects peak at road level and along canyon walls, which influence outdoor exposure and indoor infiltration, suggesting that high-resolution exposure studies should account for them.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulence closure and inflow uncertainty dominate street-canyon predictions at typical uncertainty levels, while solar forcing can dominate temperature and pollutant variability under weak ventilation when other uncertainties are reduced.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Urban exposure studies should constrain turbulence inputs while retaining thermal and vegetation effects near roads and canyon walls.
method: Run RANS simulations of a two-dimensional street canyon under two ventilation regimes.
Train a PCA–MLP surrogate for velocity, temperature, and concentration fields.
Apply global Sobol sensitivity analysis to 24 uncertain inputs while progressively narrowing nonthermal, nonvegetation uncertainties.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under weak ventilation, solar forcing dominates temperature variance when other uncertainties are halved and concentration variance when quartered; under strong ventilation, vegetation never overtakes closure constants, even with the dominant constant constrained to ±5%.
infographic.watch_item: Thresholds come from a two-dimensional RANS-based surrogate study and may not transfer directly to three-dimensional urban geometries.
infographic.paper_title: When does boundary-condition uncertainty outweigh thermal and vegetation effects in street canyon flow? A global sensitivity analysis of input uncertainty

title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows
authors: Tirthankar De, Sayantan Auddy, Ramit Dey, Shantanu Basu
abstract: Molecular clouds exhibit complex, multi-scale dynamics driven by the interplay of turbulence, self-gravity, and gas pressure. Modelling these systems with conventional grid-based methods becomes increasingly expensive as spatial resolution and dimensionality increase. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative by incorporating the governing equations directly into the training objective, but their ability to model realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows remains largely unexplored. We apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, considering subsonic and supersonic evolution in two and three dimensions. We benchmark the predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++. PINNs accurately recover the global evolution of the flow over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities. Their training cost also exhibits weak dependence on spatial resolution, increasing by less than 25% from 128^3 to 1024^3 in our experiments. These results demonstrate that PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously explored and provide a promising complementary framework for studying these systems.

infographic.key_insight: PINNs reproduce the global evolution of multidimensional turbulent, self-gravitating gas while showing weak training-cost dependence on spatial resolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This mesh-free approach offers a potential complement to grid-based solvers for computationally demanding compressible, self-gravitating flows.
method: Embed governing equations for isothermal, self-gravitating gas in the neural-network training objective.
Model subsonic and supersonic turbulent evolution in two and three dimensions.
Benchmark predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate global evolution over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities, with training cost increasing by less than 25% from 128³ to 1024³.
infographic.watch_item: Global agreement does not establish accuracy for localized shocks or collapsing structures; these require targeted error and conservation checks.
infographic.paper_title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows

title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!
authors: Maximilian Plattner, Fabian Paischer, Johannes Brandstetter
abstract: The three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid turbulence, a chaotic and non-linear physical phenomenon characterized by complex eddies interacting across vast spatial and temporal scales. A numerically accurate modeling of this multi-scale energy cascade requires fully resolving both the fine spatial structures and the continuous temporal evolution of the flow field. In this paper, we leverage massive, time-resolved direct numerical simulations, which exceed 28 TB per run, to assess how numerical choices govern the resolved (3+1)-dimensional physics of turbulent flows. Building on this analysis, we study how neural networks represent the recorded turbulent motion. Our results highlight that spatial and temporal assessments can disagree for both numerical records and learned representations. We therefore call on the machine learning community to treat (3+1)-dimensional turbulence as a four-dimensional phenomenon.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulence must be assessed in both space and time, because spatial and temporal evaluations can disagree for numerical records and neural representations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable turbulence modeling requires resolving fine spatial structures and continuous temporal evolution, rather than relying on spatial fidelity alone.
method: Analyze time-resolved direct numerical simulations of three-dimensional turbulence.
Assess how numerical choices affect resolved space–time physics.
Study how neural networks represent the recorded turbulent motion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study uses simulation runs exceeding 28 TB each and reports disagreement between spatial and temporal assessments for both numerical records and learned representations.
infographic.watch_item: The massive data volume makes storage and processing substantial implementation concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Let's Do Turbulence Right: In Space and Time!

title: A Priori Estimation of the Non-Linear Compression Potential and Quantification of Autoencoder Non-Linearity in Turbulent Flows
authors: Niklas Alexander Pissarski, Juan Pablo Murcia Leon, Søren Juhl Andersen
abstract: Data-driven reduced-order modelling (ROM) of turbulent flows is based on an efficient and physical low-dimensional representation of the flow process. Such a dimension reduction can be achieved using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) or non-linear autoencoders. Capturing the inherent non-linearities in turbulent flows offers the potential for improved compression rates. This work proposes the local tangent residual (LTR) as an a priori estimate of the potential benefit of non-linear dimension reduction for a given dataset. The LTR is based on the local geometry of the data points, requiring neither prior model training nor the definition of a threshold parameter. For all datasets investigated in this work, namely, two vortex street cases and the turbulent wake flow of a wind turbine, the dominant trends in autoencoder compression performance are reproduced by the proposed LTR. The results are further contextualised through the decoder linearisation error (DLE). The DLE quantifies the non-linearity of the trained decoder by comparing it to a linearised surrogate model, which enables physical interpretability of the non-linearities. Together, a large non-linear compression potential in the turbulent flow, as quantified by the LTR, is corroborated by a large DLE, i.e., a pronounced non-linearity captured in the trained autoencoder. The LTR thus enables practitioners in turbulent flow modelling to determine a priori whether non-linear compression is worthwhile, avoiding the substantial computational cost of autoencoder architecture search and hyperparameter tuning in cases where POD already suffices.

infographic.key_insight: The local tangent residual (LTR) estimates whether turbulent-flow data can benefit from nonlinear compression before training an autoencoder.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LTR can help practitioners avoid costly autoencoder architecture searches and hyperparameter tuning when POD already provides sufficient compression.
method: Estimate nonlinear compression potential from local data geometry using LTR, without model training or a threshold parameter.
Quantify trained decoder nonlinearity using decoder linearisation error (DLE), comparing the decoder with a linearised surrogate.
Relate LTR and DLE to autoencoder compression performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two vortex street cases and a wind-turbine turbulent wake, LTR reproduced dominant trends in autoencoder compression performance, while large LTR was corroborated by large DLE.
infographic.watch_item: Validation in the abstract is limited to three flow cases; generalisation to other turbulent-flow datasets remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: A Priori Estimation of the Non-Linear Compression Potential and Quantification of Autoencoder Non-Linearity in Turbulent Flows

title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows
authors: Tom Moussie, Pierric Joseph, Marcello Meldi
abstract: This work presents the development and assessment of a hybrid framework coupling numerical simulation, experimental samples, data assimilation (DA) and machine learning (ML) to investigate the flow within an axial compressor stage. The methodology first implements a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MFEnKF) which integrates experimental PIV data with a two-fidelity numerical simulation setup, combining steady-state RANS on a fixed grid with unsteady hybrid RANS/LES simulations on a moving grid. This data assimilation step successfully reduces discrepancies between experiments and CFD realizations. Besides, it provides additional high fidelity samples when compared with the available PIV data. This enriched database is used to train machine learning (ML) tools, with the objective to obtain black-box forcing terms to be included in the discretized form of the Navier-Stokes equations. These models are expected to preserve the accuracy of the DA results while not longer requiring the input of experimental data. The neural network architecture used here maps local physical features such as the velocity, the velocity gradients and the turbulent viscosity, to obtain the volume forcing terms. The analysis of the performance of such ML models shows that global accuracy is preserved but localized increased errors in specific regions of the compressor, such as close to the blade tips, can exceed those observed from the baseline RANS simulations. To resolve this issue, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) method is employed, which classifies and combines the trained ML tools for different flow regions. The discrepancy with experimental data of this method is systematically lower than the one observed for the baseline RANS solution and very similar to the one obtained with the MFEnKF.

infographic.key_insight: Region-aware Mixture of Experts forcing models approach data-assimilation accuracy for axial-compressor flow while avoiding experimental-data input during deployment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learned corrections could improve baseline RANS predictions for turbomachinery flows without requiring ongoing experimental measurements.
method: Fuse PIV measurements, fixed-grid steady RANS and moving-grid hybrid RANS/LES using a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter.
Train neural networks on the enriched database to map local velocity, velocity gradients and turbulent viscosity to discrete Navier–Stokes forcing terms.
Use a Mixture of Experts to select and combine learned models across flow regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against experimental data, the Mixture of Experts shows systematically lower discrepancies than baseline RANS and results very similar to MFEnKF, although the abstract reports no numerical error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Standalone neural models can produce blade-tip errors exceeding baseline RANS; performance beyond the studied compressor conditions remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows

title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
authors: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

infographic.key_insight: For geometry-aware hemodynamic surrogates, active learning and finite-element physical consistency are more effective during fine-tuning than early or continuous training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports scalable prediction of patient-specific aortic velocity and pressure fields toward real-time cardiovascular assessment.
method: Generate synthetic aortic CFD solutions with automatically adjusted physiological boundary conditions.
Represent anatomies as displacement fields from a common reference and train Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogates.
Investigate active learning and differentiable finite-element residual constraints to improve data efficiency and accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Peak-systolic evaluations show fine-tuning benefits from gradient- and subspace-based acquisition and physical consistency constraints, while out-of-distribution tests identify geometric coverage as the main limitation.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization remains limited by the geometric support of the anatomy parametrization; architectural changes alone may not address unseen shapes.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics

title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
authors: Takeru Hasegawa, Naoto Mitsume, Shota Deguchi, Mitsuteru Asai, Tetsuya Kanagawa
abstract: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.

infographic.key_insight: Sensitivity analysis helps anticipate which bubbly-liquid parameters a physics-informed neural network can recover from nonlinear waveforms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support characterization of bubbly media for ultrasound-based biomedical and industrial applications.
method: Model weakly nonlinear wave propagation with a Korteweg–de Vries–Burgers equation.
Assess eight physical parameters through coefficient- and solution-level sensitivity analysis.
Use a physics-informed neural network for forward prediction and seven single-parameter inverse estimations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The PINN reproduced the reference solution and estimated viscosity, initial bubble radius, density, sound speed, and pressure with 0.8–2.1% errors; the polytropic exponent converged partially, while surface tension estimation failed.
infographic.watch_item: Single-parameter recovery does not establish reliable simultaneous estimation, especially for weakly sensitive parameters.
infographic.paper_title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks

title: CoPiT: A conditional Position-induced Transformer for aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes
authors: Junfeng Chen, Yongchen Fan, Zhonghua Qiao, Kailiang Wu
abstract: High-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations remain a standard tool for aerodynamic analysis, yet each solve on an unstructured mesh is computationally expensive, making many-query tasks such as design exploration, optimization, and multi-condition evaluation costly. Neural operators provide mesh-flexible surrogates for mapping geometry and operating conditions to flow fields; however, in many existing architectures, global parameters such as the freestream state and design variables are concatenated with pointwise inputs, leaving their influence on intermediate features implicit. This paper proposes CoPiT, a \textbf{Co}nditional \textbf{P}osition-induced \textbf{T}ransformer that builds on the Position-induced Transformer (PiT) as its geometric backbone and injects a global condition vector through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), thereby making parametric modulation explicit while preserving geometry-based attention weights. The model is evaluated on two-dimensional AirfRANS airfoil fields, including scarce-data and extrapolation regimes, and on three-dimensional BlendedNet++ blended-wing-body surfaces. On the AirfRANS full-data test set, CoPiT reduces surface and volume losses by approximately 54\% and 24\% relative to Transolver, respectively, and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among the compared baselines on BlendedNet++. Matched ablations show that FiLM conditioning generally improves upon input concatenation, while the preferred placement is task-dependent. CoPiT thus provides a practical operator-learning surrogate for parametric aerodynamics on unstructured meshes.

infographic.key_insight: CoPiT explicitly conditions geometry-based attention features on global parameters to improve aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This surrogate could reduce reliance on expensive RANS solves during aerodynamic design exploration, optimization, and multi-condition evaluation.
method: Uses a Position-induced Transformer backbone for unstructured-mesh geometry.
Injects global operating and design conditions through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM).
Preserves geometry-based attention weights while modulating intermediate features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on 2D AirfRANS and 3D BlendedNet++, CoPiT reduces AirfRANS full-data surface and volume losses by approximately 54% and 24% versus Transolver and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among compared BlendedNet++ baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The preferred FiLM placement is task-dependent, so conditioning stages may require tuning for each application.
infographic.paper_title: CoPiT: A conditional Position-induced Transformer for aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes

title: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) approximations of capillary menisci in polygonal channels
authors: Zijian Liu, Julian Olszewski, Jie Xu
abstract: In a zero-gravity cylindrical container, a meniscus can span a square or equilateral-triangular cross-section only at contact angles at or above the respective Concus-Finn critical angles of 45 degrees and 60 degrees. We study strong-form physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across these thresholds under fixed collocation and optimization budgets. Classical capillary flux balance yields a lower bound on the combined interior and wall residual loss for arbitrary positive sampling densities. In the tested nonexistence regime, several degrees below the critical angles, independently evaluated network losses are 1.6-1.9 times this bound. A polynomial least-squares comparison supports the same geometric interpretation. The PINNs still return smooth graphs with finite axial extent, even though the prescribed equilibrium problem has no spanning graph solution. Their small interior residuals coexist with wall-flux deficits near corners, where adjoining contact-angle conditions demand more flux than a finite-slope graph can supply. Residuals vary on both sides of the critical angle, while the bound tends uniformly to zero at threshold for fixed wall weight. These results give a geometric scale for interpreting the computed loss and locate the incompatibility that a small interior residual can conceal.

infographic.key_insight: PINNs can produce smooth, finite meniscus graphs even when no spanning equilibrium solution exists, hiding geometric incompatibility in wall-flux deficits near corners.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Capillary simulations in polygonal channels need boundary-flux checks because small interior residuals alone do not establish a physically admissible meniscus.
method: Test strong-form PINNs across the 45° square and 60° equilateral-triangle critical contact angles.
Derive a capillary-flux lower bound on combined interior and wall residual loss.
Compare with polynomial least-squares approximations under fixed sampling and optimization budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Several degrees below the critical angles, independently evaluated PINN losses were 1.6–1.9 times the theoretical lower bound, with polynomial least-squares results supporting the same geometric interpretation.
infographic.watch_item: The reported loss ratios apply to tested nonexistence cases; residual magnitudes alone are not a universal existence test, especially as the bound vanishes at threshold.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) approximations of capillary menisci in polygonal channels

title: A novel machine learning framework based on proper orthogonal decomposition for turbine wake flow predictions in natural waterways
authors: Mustafa Meriç Aksen, Hossein Seyedzadeh, Mehrshad Gholami Anjiraki, Ali Khosronejad
abstract: We developed a machine learning (ML) surrogate trained on instantaneous large eddy simulation (LES) data filtered using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) to predict mean flow fields in natural rivers with complex geometries. The surrogate enables efficient prediction of mean flow fields downstream of marine hydrokinetic (MHK) turbine arrays at a fraction of the computational cost of high fidelity simulations, facilitating turbine layout optimization in natural waterways where bathymetry, turbulence, and turbine interactions influence the available energy resource. We demonstrate the capabilities of the model at a real world tidal river site under ebb tide conditions. Complex bed bathymetry and planform geometry generate substantial background turbulence that can obscure turbine wake signatures. POD is employed to extract relevant flow structures, improving the ability of the ML model to learn wake dynamics. First, LES is performed at the tidal site to generate training data. POD is then applied to decompose the instantaneous LES fields into spatial modes. Selected modes are used to train a three dimensional convolutional encoder decoder network to predict time averaged velocity fields. This selective filtering reduces the influence of dominant background fluctuations while preserving information relevant to turbine wakes. At equivalent network size and training cost, the POD filtered surrogate reduces the mean squared error by three orders of magnitude compared with the same network trained on unfiltered LES data.

infographic.key_insight: POD filtering helps a machine learning surrogate distinguish turbine wakes from background turbulence, reducing prediction error by three orders of magnitude versus training on unfiltered LES data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast predictions of mean flow downstream of marine hydrokinetic turbine arrays could support layout optimization in natural waterways with complex bathymetry.
method: Generate instantaneous flow fields using large eddy simulation (LES).
Apply proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and select modes that preserve wake-relevant structures.
Train a 3D convolutional encoder–decoder to predict time-averaged velocity fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: At a real-world tidal river site under ebb tide conditions, the POD-filtered surrogate achieved three orders of magnitude lower mean squared error at equivalent network size and training cost.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability to other sites, tidal conditions, and turbine layouts is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A novel machine learning framework based on proper orthogonal decomposition for turbine wake flow predictions in natural waterways

title: DiffVortex: A quantum-inspired fast solver for incompressible flows
authors: Yu Jun Loo, Silas Alben, Shravan Veerapaneni
abstract: Matrix-product-state (MPS) and quantized tensor-train (QTT) representations offer a promising framework for computational fluid dynamics, with logarithmic run time and memory scaling in mesh size when bond dimensions remain bounded. Existing MPS-based solvers are Eulerian: they compress velocity fields and enforce immersed-body boundary conditions through static masks or body-fitted coordinates. Moving or flexible bodies complicate this approach: deformation requires updating MPS masks every time step, while filamentary vorticity in high-Reynolds-number flows may resist low-rank compression. We propose a complementary approach: compress the Biot--Savart kernel rather than the flow state, evolve vorticity using Lagrangian vortex particles, and represent immersed bodies by bound vortex sheets on Lagrangian surface points. Our main theoretical result is a lifting theorem: QTT rank $r$ of the kernel implies matrix-product-operator (MPO) rank at most $2^d r$ for the corresponding convolution operator in $d$ dimensions, independent of grid resolution. This bound is sharp for our interleaved ordering. With quantics tensor cross interpolation, the moment-to-local stage of a single-level fast multipole method becomes a precomputed tensor-network contraction with quasi-linear complexity, retaining Lagrangian flexibility for immersed bodies. Our PyTorch implementation (\texttt{DiffVortex}) is end-to-end differentiable, runs on GPUs, and handles $6.7\times10^{7}$ particles on a single device. We validate against reference vortex-method results for an impulsively started cylinder and exact and reference solutions for inviscid elliptical vortices. We also demonstrate two-dimensional flows past rigidly moving, multiple, and deforming bodies, including gradients propagated through the full time integration.

infographic.key_insight: DiffVortex compresses the Biot–Savart kernel rather than the flow state, combining tensor-network acceleration with Lagrangian flexibility for moving and deforming bodies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its differentiable GPU implementation supports large-scale vortex simulations and gradient propagation through time integration for potential flow-design applications.
method: Evolve vorticity with Lagrangian particles and represent immersed bodies with bound vortex sheets.
Use quantics tensor cross interpolation to precompute tensor-network contractions for fast-multipole moment-to-local interactions.
Prove that kernel QTT rank r yields convolution MPO rank at most 2^d r, independent of grid resolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 6.7×10^7 particles on one GPU, validation on an impulsively started cylinder and inviscid elliptical vortices, and demonstrations with moving, multiple, and deforming bodies.
infographic.watch_item: Efficiency depends on compressible kernel representations; the abstract does not establish comparable performance for general three-dimensional engineering flows.
infographic.paper_title: DiffVortex: A quantum-inspired fast solver for incompressible flows

title: CARS: a centerline-anchored attention surrogate for coronary blood flow on skeleton-generated lumen geometries
authors: Reza Akbarian Bafghi, Sukirt Thakur, Maziar Raissi
abstract: When the parameter of a PDE surrogate is the flow domain itself, the key/value set of an attention model must encode that domain. We present CARS (Coronary Artery Rapid Surrogate), a learned surrogate for the finite-volume solution map of the steady incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on coronary lumens built from image-derived centerlines. CARS maps a centerline with per-point lumen radius and a scalar inlet flow rate to pressure and velocity at arbitrary query points. The attention focal set is the case's own centerline, so geometry fusion costs $O(N n_f)$ rather than $O(N^2)$ in the number of evaluation points. Trained per territory on $2{,}700$ OpenFOAM solutions with synthetic focal lesions, CARS reaches relative $\ell_2$ errors of $0.120/0.149$ (pressure/velocity) on left-coronary and $0.063/0.119$ on right-coronary test sets, in $87$~ms per case against a solver wall-clock of $572$-$1{,}063$~s. It outperforms four parameter-matched neural operators, and accuracy saturates eightfold below the operating focal count. Fractional flow reserve derived from the predicted pressure matches the CFD label at Pearson $r = 0.941/0.993$ and reproduces the $\mathrm{FFR}\le 0.8$ decision in $97.7\%/96.3\%$ of held-out cases. The predicted velocity does not satisfy continuity closely enough for derived quantities, and the weights are territory-specific.

infographic.key_insight: CARS anchors attention to coronary centerlines to rapidly predict pressure and velocity across variable lumen geometries.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables coronary flow evaluation in 87 ms per case versus 572–1,063 s for CFD, with strong agreement on pressure-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR).
method: Inputs: image-derived centerline, per-point lumen radius, and scalar inlet flow rate.
Predicts steady incompressible flow pressure and velocity at arbitrary query points.
Uses centerline-anchored attention with O(N n_f) geometry-fusion cost rather than O(N²).
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained per territory on 2,700 OpenFOAM solutions with synthetic lesions, CARS achieved left/right test relative ℓ₂ errors of 0.120/0.063 for pressure and 0.149/0.119 for velocity, with 97.7%/96.3% agreement on the FFR ≤ 0.8 decision.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted velocity does not satisfy continuity closely enough for derived quantities, and model weights are territory-specific.
infographic.paper_title: CARS: a centerline-anchored attention surrogate for coronary blood flow on skeleton-generated lumen geometries

title: Swarmlet: a GPU-resident reformulated vortex particle method for coupled multirotor aerodynamics and flight dynamics
authors: Wyatt James Horne
abstract: We present Swarmlet, a GPU solver for the unsteady aerodynamics and flight dynamics of one or many multirotor vehicles. The wake is a meshless, evolving-core vortex particle field in the reformulated (rVPM) large-eddy formulation, coupled to rotor models of three fidelities, six-degree-of-freedom vehicles and flight control. Particles carry a smooth core of compact support whose field outside four core radii is exactly the singular Biot-Savart field, so the multipole far field of the treecode carries no regularization error. The subfilter closure is a dynamic eddy viscosity on a fixed filter width, applied by core spreading with a Lagrangian exchange of its local excess under an explicit stability bound, and the strengths are relaxed by projection; global corrections make both the exchange and the relaxation conserve total vorticity and linear impulse. All rotor models shed connected bound circulation, the disks along the arcs swept in each step however long, so the wake receives the lift impulse. The solver agrees with direct summation to $5\times 10^{-7}$ and converges at third order in time. Without calibration, an actuator-line model that includes its own near sheet predicts the hover thrust of a DJI 9443 propeller within 2%. With calibrated section polars it reproduces a Crazyflie propeller's thrust and torque within 3.2% at three speeds and the near wake of a hovering quadrotor with relative $L^2$ differences of 0.08-0.21 against particle image velocimetry, while the wake keeps the delivered impulse. A closed-loop formation of 100 quadrotors, run at a coarser setting on one GPU, illustrates the coupled method at swarm scale.

infographic.key_insight: Swarmlet couples GPU-resident vortex-particle aerodynamics with flight dynamics and control to simulate multirotor wakes from individual propellers to 100-vehicle formations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The solver supports analysis of rotor performance, wake interactions and closed-loop multirotor formations on a single GPU.
method: Meshless reformulated vortex particle LES with compact-support cores and a treecode far field free of regularization error.
Dynamic eddy viscosity, core spreading and strength relaxation with corrections conserving total vorticity and linear impulse.
Three rotor-model fidelities coupled to six-degree-of-freedom vehicles and flight control, with connected circulation shedding.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported tests show agreement with direct summation to 5×10⁻⁷, third-order time convergence, hover thrust within 2% without calibration, calibrated thrust and torque within 3.2%, and near-wake relative L² differences of 0.08–0.21 against particle image velocimetry.
infographic.watch_item: The 100-quadrotor demonstration uses a coarser setting; the abstract does not establish swarm-scale accuracy comparable to the propeller and near-wake validation.
infographic.paper_title: Swarmlet: a GPU-resident reformulated vortex particle method for coupled multirotor aerodynamics and flight dynamics

title: Compression of turbulent flow data through an extended space-time correlation: certification against the modal energy budget
authors: Gustavo Lopes, Davide Lengani, Dan Henningson
abstract: The fidelity of direct numerical simulation now outpaces the storage and data-movement capacity available for the resulting fields. We present an open, distributed, GPU-accelerated low-rank compression framework for large turbulent flow databases. We assess it using two direct numerical simulations of a controlled diffusion compressor cascade under laminar and turbulent inflow conditions. Compression is formulated using a correlation operator over space and time, which is two orders of magnitude larger than that of snapshot POD. Its dominant range is extracted with a randomized range finder based on communication-avoiding hierarchical QR. The compressed databases are evaluated through a hierarchy of increasingly strict diagnostics, from instantaneous reconstruction and second-order statistics to the modal turbulent kinetic energy budget and its nonlinear interscale transfer. The budget terms are far more sensitive to compression than fieldwise or one-point errors. They remain accurate at conservative compression and degrade sharply once the retained energy is relaxed. The near-wall dissipation and the interscale transfer degrade the most and set the admissible compression level. An aggressive reduction preserves every one-point statistic to within a few per cent while corrupting both by an order of magnitude more. The dissipation error is confined to the viscous sublayer and grows with the development of the boundary layer. It is carried by the high-order modes. For both inflows, the linear budget terms scale with the discarded energy to the power $0.8$ and the triadic transfer to a power above one.

infographic.key_insight: Low-rank compression can preserve turbulent-flow statistics while substantially corrupting near-wall dissipation and nonlinear interscale energy transfer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Modal energy-budget checks help set compression limits for large DNS databases when accurate turbulence physics matters more than fieldwise reconstruction alone.
method: Construct an extended space-time correlation operator roughly 100 times larger than snapshot POD's.
Extract its dominant range using a randomized range finder with communication-avoiding hierarchical QR.
Use a distributed, GPU-accelerated framework and validate reconstructions against statistics and modal energy budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on compressor-cascade DNS with laminar and turbulent inflows show that aggressive compression preserves all one-point statistics within a few percent while producing roughly an order of magnitude larger errors in dissipation and interscale transfer.
infographic.watch_item: Do not select compression levels from retained energy or one-point statistics alone: high-order modes carry near-wall dissipation that these checks can miss.
infographic.paper_title: Compression of turbulent flow data through an extended space-time correlation: certification against the modal energy budget

title: Heat vortices and the vorticity triplet in kinetic phonon transport: a fluid-dynamical perspective
authors: Tao Chen, Chuang Zhang, Tianshu Liu
abstract: From a novel fluid-dynamical perspective, the present study investigates the heat-current vortices and heat vorticity in heat conduction process of solid materials. The heat vorticity $\bmω$, defined as the curl of the heat-flux field, is decomposed into the orbital-rotation $\bm{R}$ and spin $\bm{S}$, which collectively constitute the heat-vorticity triplet $(\bm{R},\bm{S},\bmω)$, extending beyond the existing single-vorticity research paradigm. As an illustrative example, kinetic phonon transport in a 2D porous solid structure is examined based on the numerical solutions of the Peierls-Boltzmann equation under the Callway dual-relaxation-time approximation. The physical characteristics of heat vortices and the vorticity triplet patterns are analyzed across different kinetic regimes in the phase diagram of the normal (N) and resistive (R) scattering processes.... In the hydrodynamic limit, the boundary generation mechanism of heat vorticity is further elucidated based on the Guyer-Krumhansl (G-K) equation generated from the truncated Chapman-Enskog (C-E) expansion. The boundary heat vorticity flux (BHVF) is proposed as a new concept for describing the local rate at which heat vorticity is generated at the boundary of a solid material. The general expression for the BHVF is rigorously derived for phonon hydrodynamics, and for the 2D steady hydrodynamic phonon transport case, we find that the BHVF is solely attributed to the tangential component of the net heat flux deviating from the classical Fourier heat flux. Furthermore, we show that the total vorticity contained in a control volume arises from the spatiotemporal accumulation of the BHVF, weighted by the memory kernel arising from the R scattering. The proposed theory and findings herein could be valuable for understanding the diverse vortical-flow phenomena in condensed matter systems.

infographic.key_insight: Heat-current vortices are characterized by a triplet of orbital rotation, spin, and heat vorticity, with boundary-generated vorticity linked to departures from Fourier conduction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework could help interpret non-Fourier heat transport in porous solids where phonon hydrodynamics and boundary effects matter.
method: Solve the Peierls–Boltzmann equation with a dual-relaxation-time approximation for a 2D porous solid.
Analyze heat vortices and vorticity-triplet patterns across normal and resistive scattering regimes.
Derive boundary heat-vorticity flux from the Guyer–Krumhansl equation in the hydrodynamic limit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical kinetic-transport analysis and analytical boundary-flux derivations, but provides no quantitative benchmarks or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: The result linking boundary vorticity generation solely to tangential non-Fourier heat flux applies specifically to steady 2D hydrodynamic phonon transport.
infographic.paper_title: Heat vortices and the vorticity triplet in kinetic phonon transport: a fluid-dynamical perspective

title: Tandem jets in crossflow: the enclosed-recirculation momentum exchange and the unsteady shear-layer dynamics
authors: Xunchen Liu
abstract: Twin tandem jets in crossflow are examined by 40\ kHz time-resolved particle image velocimetry (PIV) over nine spacing--velocity-ratio conditions ($L=2d$--$4d$, $r\approx3$--7; 68 twin cases, 11 single-jet records). The front jet is diluted: its trajectory lies below the single-jet reference, with a near-field segment up to 40\% shorter, and its velocity ratio falls to an effective value $r_{\mathrm{eff}}<r$, while the shielded rear jet rises above the reference. This paper identifies the carrier of that dilution and the unsteady dynamics that sustains it. The rear-jet blockage closes a gap recirculation whose reversed flow puts the two gap-side layers in the counter-current shear-layer configuration, the classical route to enhanced entrainment. The measured Reynolds stress and Prandtl mixing length show that the absolute exchange is nearly independent of the velocity ratio and exceeds the single-jet leeward zone like-for-like by up to $1.5\times$ (zone peak, across conditions) and $2.8\times$ (area-integrated) at $r\approx7$. The gain comes from an enlarged mixing scale rather than from a steeper shear, and the front-jet near-field shortening follows the absolute exchange transport rather than the twin/single enhancement ratio. The turbulent term exceeds the pressure term in eight of the nine conditions, and the flux budget reads the dilution as a limited mass addition plus a momentum loss to the crossflow; the evidence remains observational. The gap-side layers remain convectively unstable---DMD and SPOD find no growing mode within the resolvable band and record length---so the exchange is carried by convecting vortex trains rather than by a self-excited global mode.

infographic.key_insight: Rear-jet blockage encloses a recirculation zone that enhances momentum exchange through larger mixing scales, diluting the front jet while the shielded rear jet rises higher.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tandem-jet designs should account for gap-driven momentum loss rather than assume that each jet follows an isolated-jet trajectory.
method: 40 kHz time-resolved PIV across nine spacing–velocity-ratio conditions.
Reynolds-stress, mixing-length and flux-budget analysis.
DMD and SPOD analysis of unsteady shear-layer dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 68 twin-jet cases and 11 single-jet records, front-jet near-field segments were up to 40% shorter, while gap exchange reached 2.8× the single-jet leeward-zone area-integrated value at r ≈ 7.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism is supported observationally; no growing mode was detected only within the resolvable frequency band and available record length.
infographic.paper_title: Tandem jets in crossflow: the enclosed-recirculation momentum exchange and the unsteady shear-layer dynamics

title: CBTV: Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry for Dense Granular Flows
authors: Kaveeshan Thurairajah, Zhao Pan
abstract: Conventional particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) has been the standard diagnostic tool for studying fluid and granular flows. However, in dense granular systems, the average distance moved by particles between frames can approach or exceed inter-particle spacing, demanding ultra-high frame rates. Furthermore, neighbouring particles may move together, and common velocity-based prediction fails after energetic collisions. Existing methods struggle to track granular particles without losing identities or swapping. We present Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry (CBTV), a training-free multi-pass method leveraging multicoloured particles to achieve enhanced tracking. CBTV first matches constellations of neighbouring coloured particles as single units, guided by a cross-correlation motion prior, and only then assigns the remaining particles individually. We compare it with 12 baseline tracker configurations, from classical linkers to graph-neural-network and transformer models, on 59 cases from 15 simulated discrete-element granular flows with exact ground truth (0.006-9 diameters/frame). CBTV matches or exceeds every tracker tested on an impulsive collision at every displacement. Its advantage lies in dense flows in which particles move between about half and twice their spacing per frame, where links between frames are ambiguous. On agitated shear flow, a colour relaxation tracker, which also uses neighbour context, matches or narrowly exceeds CBTV. Where links are unambiguous, CBTV is close to the best tracker, and beyond about two to three particle diameters per frame, the range of its motion prior, trackers that compensate for bulk motion are more accurate. For experimentalists, dense granular flows of coloured particles can be tracked at displacements per frame where trackers without neighbour context lose identities, easing the demand for ultra-high frame rates without training data.

infographic.key_insight: CBTV preserves particle identities in dense granular flows by tracking coloured neighbour constellations before linking individual particles.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For experiments with coloured grains, CBTV can ease ultra-high-frame-rate requirements when particles move roughly half to twice their spacing between frames.
method: Use cross-correlation to estimate a motion prior.
Match neighbouring coloured particles as constellations.
Assign remaining particles individually in a training-free, multi-pass workflow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation against 12 baseline tracker configurations on 59 cases from 15 simulated granular flows with exact ground truth found CBTV matched or exceeded every baseline on impulsive collisions at all tested displacements.
infographic.watch_item: Beyond roughly 2–3 particle diameters per frame, CBTV's motion prior becomes limiting, and bulk-motion-compensating trackers are more accurate.
infographic.paper_title: CBTV: Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry for Dense Granular Flows

title: Extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method
authors: Luís Orlando Emerich dos Santos, Diogo Nardelli Siebert
abstract: Regularized lattice Boltzmann methods improve numerical stability by projecting the nonequilibrium distribution onto its hydrodynamic second-order Hermite sector and filtering the remaining kinetic modes. We introduce a separate relaxation time for the complete complementary kinetic subspace. The resulting extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method (E-RLBM) interpolates continuously between the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook and regularized collision operators while retaining a two-rate implementation. A Chapman-Enskog expansion shows that the isothermal Navier-Stokes equations are recovered with kinematic viscosity $ν=c_s^2(τ-Δt/2)$, independently of the kinetic relaxation time $τ_{\rm nh}$, whereas $τ_{\rm nh}$ changes higher-order truncation errors. For linear transverse shear, its first effect is a fourth-derivative term whose coefficient depends on the direction of propagation relative to the lattice. This fourth-order coefficient is affine in $τ_{\rm nh}$. For linear shear on D2Q9 and $τ_{\rm nh}$ between $τ$ and $Δt$, it lies between the corresponding BGK and RLBM values in every propagation direction. Stability maps for the decaying Taylor-Green vortex and flow past a rectangular obstacle show that an appropriate kinetic relaxation substantially enlarges the stable parameter domain. In a Taylor-Green convergence test with consistent initialization, all three operators converge at second order, and their error differences follow the hyperviscous coefficient for diagonal shear waves: the E-RLBM error is about 6% above the BGK error and about 40% below the RLBM error; in a double shear layer at Re = 80000, the E-RLBM follows the RLBM convergence curve. The proposed collision operator therefore provides a low-cost means of controlling nonhydrodynamic modes without introducing a full multiple-relaxation-time basis.

infographic.key_insight: E-RLBM independently relaxes nonhydrodynamic modes, continuously bridging BGK and regularized collision operators without changing Navier–Stokes viscosity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A low-cost, two-rate collision operator can enlarge the stable simulation domain without requiring a full multiple-relaxation-time basis.
method: Project nonequilibrium distributions onto the second-order hydrodynamic Hermite sector.
Apply a separate relaxation time to the complete complementary kinetic subspace.
Use Chapman–Enskog and linear shear analysis to characterize viscosity and higher-order errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Taylor–Green vortex and obstacle-flow tests show improved stability; all three operators achieve second-order Taylor–Green convergence, with E-RLBM error about 6% above BGK and 40% below RLBM.
infographic.watch_item: Kinetic relaxation changes direction-dependent fourth-order shear errors, so stability gains require attention to accuracy and parameter selection.
infographic.paper_title: Extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method
